one_liner: C++17 policy-based logger with allocation-free log calls and an SPSC/MPSC ring-buffer async mode; README claims 2.5-20x over spdlog.
what_it_does: A spdlog-style logger: you create a logger with sinks (stdout, stderr, file, custom) and call info/debug/critical with {}-style placeholders and a user-defined pattern with colors, alignment, topics and custom attributes. The logger type is a long template: buffer limits, sync or async execution policy, flush policy, threading policy and a compile-time sink list (runtime sinks also supported). Convenience aliases cover the common cases, with _mt variants for thread safety. It is not source-compatible with spdlog.
how_it_is_fast: Log calls format into fixed-size pre-allocated buffers whose sizes are template parameters (pattern 256, message 128, argument 64, 4 args by default), so no heap allocation per call. The pattern is parsed once when set and compiled into a list of formatters, so the call site only substitutes values. Async mode is a bounded ring buffer (default 1024 slots) with cache-line-aligned read/write indices; SPSC uses plain atomics, the thread-safe variant takes an atomic_flag spinlock on enqueue (MPSC), and the worker thread spins with an adaptive waiter. Producers enqueue only the format-string pointer, source metadata and argument strings converted to chars; formatting happens on the worker.
when_to_use: Single-producer async logging to console or file where call-site latency matters and messages fit the static buffer limits
Embedded or real-time code that must avoid heap allocation in the logging path
Projects that already pick sinks and policies at compile time and want spdlog-like {} formatting without the fmt dependency
Buffered sync logging to a stream where losing unflushed lines on crash is acceptable
when_not_to_use: Messages or arguments longer than the configured limits (128-byte message, 64-byte argument, 4 arguments by default); the limits are fixed at compile time
Many producer threads: the MPSC queue is a spinlock around a ring buffer, not a lock-free multi-producer queue, and no multi-thread benchmark is published
When you need reproducible evidence: the picobench harness used for the README tables is not in the repository (Sandbox/ holds only a timer demo), and no compiler, flags or CPU are given
Drop-in replacement for spdlog call sites or for nanosecond-class loggers such as Quill, fmtlog or NanoLog
Package-manager consumers: no Conan or vcpkg package (open issue #39)

integration.platforms: Windows x64 (MSVC, MinGW, Clang), Linux x64 (GCC, Clang, Intel icx) and arm64 (GCC, Clang), macOS x64 (Apple Clang), per README CI table
integration.thread_safety: Per policy: single_threaded_policy (default aliases) is not thread-safe; multi_threaded_policy and _mt aliases lock sinks with a mutex; async thread-safe mode uses a spinlock-guarded MPSC ring buffer

gotchas: Async mode queues the raw const char* format string, not a copy, so a format string built at runtime (for example std::string::c_str()) must outlive the worker thread processing it
Default flush policy is immediate_flush_policy (fflush after every log); the large README sync speedups come from buffered_flush_policy (4 MiB stream buffer) and lose unflushed lines on a crash
overwrite_last_overflow_policy advances the read index from the producer while the worker may be extracting the same slot; from code reading this looks racy, so prefer block or discard_new
The default overflow policy busy-waits with CPU pause when the 1024-slot queue is full, and the worker spins via an adaptive waiter, so expect a burning core under load
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick lwlog over Quill, fmtlog or NanoLog when you want a small, readable, allocation-free codebase with spdlog-like patterns and compile-time policies, and can live without their published, reproducible nanosecond-level latency numbers. For multi-threaded hot paths, Quill or fmtlog have better evidence.
verified_claims_summary: First-party picobench tables in the README compare lwlog with spdlog in four modes over 8 to 8192 messages: sync 7.4x at 8 messages falling to 2.5x at 8192; async blocking 16x at 8 messages and 540x at 4096, where spdlog's row jumps to 565 us/op, which suggests queue saturation rather than steady state; async nonblocking 20.7x falling to 2.4x. The 237-319x 'buffered' table pits buffered lwlog against unbuffered spdlog. No compiler, flags, CPU or benchmark source is published.
status_note: Active (last commit 2025-12-25, v1.3.0 in CMakeLists, 353 stars), MIT-licensed, five open issues and none of them bugs; small enough to vendor, but its performance claims are unreproducible first-party numbers.
